summary:
Djibouti has no statute that explicitly criminalises consensual same-sex conduct. Articles 353 and 354 of the penal code invoke "good morals" and public morality without naming same-sex relations, and no provision states the position either way. Outright International's country overview nevertheless marks same-sex relations as not lawful throughout the territory in its at-a-glance assessment, and authorities retain the power to prosecute public same-sex conduct under these articles. The practical position is that such conduct is treated as de facto illegal despite the absence of an express offence.

Public-morality and "obscene acts" provisions are used against people. No reported case law defines the outer limits of Articles 353 and 354, so the exposure of a trans visitor who is visible, or who engages in any same-sex conduct in a public setting, cannot be predicted from the text of the law.

There is no legal gender recognition in Djibouti, which affects which identity documents a trans visitor can present at entry, in hotels, or to police. LGBTI organisations cannot register, so no domestic group operates as a registered service or referral point.

Discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity is not prohibited in general terms; the only protection reported is in employment. The 2023 US State Department Human Rights Report records no legal prohibition of SOGI discrimination and no citable cases of official violence, while noting that complaints may be filed with the police or with the national human-rights commission (CNDH).

Status and conduct are treated as taboo. Pervasive social and religious intolerance means people fear family and community shunning on disclosure, and no public societal discussion of homosexuality is tolerated. A trans visitor who is read as gender-nonconforming in public therefore faces social exposure and hostility independent of any police action.
tangentialFactors:
Djibouti's position sits alongside a broader regional pattern in which same-sex conduct is either expressly prohibited or left ambiguous under residual public-morality language; the Djiboutian feature is the ambiguity itself, with the legal outcome turning on how authorities apply Articles 353 and 354 rather than on a defined offence.

The country's documentation base is thin. A Canadian Immigration and Refugee Board response to information request covering 2009 to March 2012 found that material on the treatment of sexual minorities was scarce across all consulted sources and relied largely on the US 2010 country report, indicating how little legal, protective or support framework existed in that period. The 2015 US State Department report contained only limited LGBT-specific content, its remaining sections addressing opposition suppression, prison conditions, female genital mutilation and trafficking.

The absence of registered LGBTI organisations means there is no domestic infrastructure a visitor could turn to for referral, and no parallel civil-society channel alongside the police and the CNDH.
localsOnly:
Residents have no route to legal gender recognition, so official identity documents continue to reflect the sex assigned at birth for anyone who is transgender.

LGBTI organisations cannot register, which bars formal advocacy, service provision and any organised complaint-making on these issues. Individuals may still lodge complaints with the police or with the national human-rights commission.

Protection against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity is reported only in the employment context; no general statutory prohibition applies to housing, services, education or public accommodation.

Disclosure carries a social cost. Status and conduct are treated as taboo, public discussion of homosexuality is not tolerated, and people report fear of family and community shunning, with social and religious intolerance described as pervasive.
outOfScopeNotes:
Two sources conflict on employment protection: one overview states that discrimination protection exists in employment only, while the 2023 US State Department report states that there is no legal prohibition of SOGI discrimination. The scope of any employment-based protection is unresolved on this inventory.

No case law interpreting the limits of Articles 353 and 354 is sourced, so the boundary between private conduct and prosecutable conduct is unresolved. No trans-specific violence incident, with date and outcome, appears in the inventory; the 2023 report's finding is the absence of citable official violence cases, which is not the same as a finding that no violence occurs.

Entry, visa and border-screening rules for transgender travellers, including how gender markers on foreign passports are treated, are not sourced here. Nor are facility access, healthcare provision or any specific accommodation practice. The 2015 and 2012-era reporting is retained only as historical baseline and should not be read as describing current conditions.
